bill.title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency of the Department of the Treasury relating to the review of applications under the Bank Merger Act.

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects the regulatory process banks must follow when seeking approval to merge with other banks.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would overturn a September 2024 rule from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency that changed how bank merger applications are reviewed. The rule eliminated automatic approvals for certain mergers and ended the use of simplified application forms. If this resolution passes, those procedural changes would be nullified and the prior review process would remain in effect.

bill.title: A joint resolution disapproving the rule submitted by the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection relating to "Overdraft Lending: Very Large Financial Institutions".

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects overdraft fee revenue and regulatory compliance obligations at very large financial institutions.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would nullify a Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rule that limits overdraft fees at very large banks. The rule, published in December 2024, requires these institutions to either cap overdraft charges at $5, set a higher justified amount, or treat overdrafts as credit subject to Truth in Lending Act disclosures. If enacted, the resolution would prevent the rule from taking effect, leaving existing overdraft fee practices in place.

bill.title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Internal Revenue Service relating to "Gross Proceeds Reporting by Brokers That Regularly Provide Services Effectuating Digital Asset Sales".
bill.latestActionText: Message received in Senate: Returned to the Senate pursuant to the provisions of H.Res. 212.

industries.rationale: The bill directly nullifies a reporting rule imposed on digital asset brokers and DeFi platforms, eliminating a new regulatory compliance obligation.
Traditional financial institutions that offer digital asset services would be relieved of the broker reporting requirements this rule imposed.

bill.plainSummary: This resolution would block a December 2024 IRS rule that requires brokers and platforms facilitating digital asset (cryptocurrency) sales to report transaction details and gross proceeds to the IRS. The rule was designed to improve tax compliance by ensuring the IRS receives information about cryptocurrency sales, similar to reporting requirements for stocks and other securities. If passed, the resolution would nullify this reporting requirement before it takes effect.

bill.title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection relating to "Prohibition on Creditors and Consumer Reporting Agencies Concerning Medical Information (Regulation V)".
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects lenders' ability to consider medical debt in credit eligibility decisions.
Credit reporting agencies, which include major consumer reporting bureaus, would be affected by changes to what information they may include in reports.
Hospitals and health systems that extend credit or report unpaid medical bills would be affected by whether medical debt appears on credit reports.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would overturn a Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rule published in January 2025. That rule prohibits medical debt from appearing on consumer credit reports and bars lenders from using medical debt when deciding whether to extend credit. If this resolution passes, the CFPB rule would be nullified and the prior framework would remain in effect.

bill.title: A joint resolution disapproving the rule submitted by the Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection relating to "Defining Larger Participants of a Market for General-Use Digital Consumer Payment Applications".

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects digital payment application providers by removing CFPB supervisory authority over larger platforms.
The rule targets non-bank payment processors, and nullifying it affects competitive regulatory obligations between banks and non-bank financial technology firms.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would overturn a Consumer Financial Protection Bureau rule published in December 2024. That rule gave the CFPB authority to supervise large digital payment apps—specifically, non-bank companies that process at least 50 million transactions per year. If this resolution passes, the CFPB rule would be nullified and those payment apps would not be subject to the agency's supervisory oversight.

bill.title: Fair Access to Banking Act
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.

industries.rationale: The bill directly regulates how banks and credit unions may deny financial services to customers.
Digital asset firms have frequently reported being denied banking services, making them likely beneficiaries of fair-access requirements.
Firearms businesses have reported service denials from banks citing reputational risk, which this bill would prohibit.
Cannabis and related businesses have faced banking access challenges that this bill's requirements could address.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would restrict banks, credit unions, and payment card networks from refusing service to customers who comply with the law. Financial institutions could only deny service based on documented, quantitative risk standards set in advance, and could not cite reputational concerns as a reason. Violations would trigger penalties including loss of federal deposit insurance, exclusion from electronic payment systems, and potential civil lawsuits by affected customers.

bill.title: High-Quality Charter Schools Act
bill.latestActionText: Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions. Hearings held.

industries.rationale: The bill directly subsidizes contributions to charter school organizations, expanding their funding sources and operational capacity.
The bill allows donations of market securities, which may affect how financial institutions handle charitable transfers of investment assets.

bill.plainSummary: This bill would create a federal tax credit equal to 75% of cash or securities donated to eligible charter school organizations that create or expand charter schools. Individual taxpayers could claim up to $5,000 or 10% of their adjusted gross income, whichever is greater, with unused credits carried forward for five years. The bill sets a $5 billion annual cap on total credits, with $10 million allocated to each state and the remainder distributed first-come, first-served, and requires charter organizations to spend contributions within a specified timeframe or lose eligibility.

bill.title: Combating Organized Retail Crime Act
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary.

industries.rationale: The bill directly addresses organized theft targeting retail operations and e-commerce platforms.
The bill explicitly covers theft from interstate and foreign shipments, affecting logistics and shipping companies.
The bill addresses online marketplaces and social media platforms where stolen goods are sold, potentially creating new compliance obligations.
The bill expands money laundering statutes to cover prepaid cards and gift cards, affecting payment processors and card issuers.

bill.plainSummary: This bill expands federal authority to prosecute organized retail theft and supply-chain crime. It allows prosecutors to aggregate the value of stolen goods over a 12-month period to meet felony thresholds, makes these offenses predicate crimes for money laundering charges, and authorizes asset forfeiture. The bill also creates a temporary coordination center within the Department of Homeland Security to help federal agencies work together on these cases.

bill.title: Laken Riley Act

industries.rationale: The bill directly imposes new detention mandates on DHS and creates liability exposure for federal agencies, while authorizing state governments to bring suit over immigration enforcement.

The bill creates new grounds for state litigation against the federal government and expands detention requirements, generating demand for legal services in immigration and intergovernmental litigation.

bill.plainSummary: This bill requires the Department of Homeland Security to detain certain non-citizens who are in the country unlawfully and have been arrested for or charged with crimes including burglary, theft, assault on law enforcement, or offenses causing death or serious injury. It also allows state governments to sue the federal government if immigration enforcement decisions or failures—such as releasing detainees, not conducting required asylum interviews, or violating parole limitations—cause harm to the state or its residents, including financial harm exceeding $100.

bill.title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Department of Energy relating to "Energy Conservation Program: Energy Conservation Standards for Consumer Gas-fired Instantaneous Water Heaters".
bill.latestActionText: Placed on Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders. Calendar No. 12.

industries.rationale: Manufacturers of gas-fired instantaneous water heaters would be directly affected by the nullification of energy efficiency standards that govern their product design and compliance costs.
Natural gas suppliers have a stake in standards that affect the efficiency and market competitiveness of gas-fired appliances versus electric alternatives.
Energy efficiency standards for gas appliances can influence the relative market share of gas versus electric water heating systems.
Contractors and builders who install water heaters would face different product availability and compliance requirements depending on whether the standards remain in effect.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would overturn a Department of Energy rule issued in December 2024 that set new energy efficiency standards for gas-fired instantaneous water heaters (commonly called tankless water heaters). The DOE rule required these appliances to meet stricter energy conservation requirements. If this resolution passes, the new standards would be nullified and would not take effect.

bill.title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval under chapter 8 of title 5, United States Code, of the rule submitted by the Environmental Protection Agency relating to "National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants: Rubber Tire Manufacturing".
bill.latestActionText: Read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works.

industries.rationale: The bill directly affects rubber tire manufacturers by blocking new emission standards that would impose regulatory obligations on their facilities.
Tire manufacturers supply the transportation sector, and regulatory costs or compliance changes could affect tire pricing and availability.

bill.plainSummary: This joint resolution would block an Environmental Protection Agency rule that sets emission standards for hazardous air pollutants from rubber tire manufacturing facilities. The EPA rule, published in November 2024, was designed to regulate emissions from the rubber processing part of tire manufacturing. If this resolution passes, that EPA rule would be nullified and would have no legal effect.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
